reason: The Indus was Sindh's trade artery, carrying boat cargo from the delta port past Thatta, Sehwan and Bukkur to the Panjnad confluence and on to Multan and Lahore.

sea_head.evidence: Lahari Bandar was the main sea port of Sindh from the early 1300s to the late 1600s; sea cargo was transshipped there to river boats for Thatta.

river_head.evidence: Boat traffic ran up the Indus through Sindh to where the combined Punjab rivers join it near Mithankot; above that the upper Indus carried mainly local salt and timber rafts.

head.evidence: Multan and Lahore were reached by river boats from the Indus via the Chenab and Ravi; Burnes took his 1831 mission by boat up this route to Lahore.

period_note: Thatta (tag thatta) and Sehwan/Sukkur lie on the included reach; the delta shifted often and Lahari Bandar silted after c.1700 (Karachi replaced it in the 18th century). The Attock-Kalabagh gorge reach is left out.

reason: The Ganges was the busiest inland waterway of South Asia, with large cargo boats carrying grain, saltpetre, cloth and sugar between Bengal, Patna, Varanasi and Allahabad.

sea_head.evidence: Satgaon was the chief port of southern Bengal on the Hooghly, reached by Portuguese and Asian ships (Porto Pequeno) until silting shifted trade to Hugli in the later 1500s.

river_head.evidence: Heavy river boats worked the Ganges from Bengal past Patna and Varanasi up to the Yamuna confluence at Allahabad, the natural terminus of the lower-river trade.

head.evidence: Agra, the Mughal capital on the Yamuna, was linked to Bengal by boat traffic via Allahabad; above Agra to Delhi the river was usable only seasonally.

period_note: Hooghly and Yamuna are folded into this entry. The Bhagirathi-Hooghly link to the main Ganges was seasonal and declining after c.1500; the Padma carried the main flow east to the Meghna near Sonargaon. Varanasi, Ghazipur, Patna, Monghyr and Rajmahal lie on the reach; Kanpur/Kannauj (kanauj) above Allahabad are left out.

reason: Included as the sea reach of the Ganges entry (sea_head satgaon), not a separate channel.

sea_head.evidence: Satgaon was the Hooghly port reached by sea-going ships until silting in the 16th century.

reason: Included as a Ganges branch with head Agra, not a separate channel.

sea_head.evidence: The Yamuna joins the Ganges at Allahabad; it has no sea access of its own.

period_note: See Ganges branch; Delhi (river level 2 in game) was reachable only seasonally.

reason: The Meghna-Brahmaputra carried Bengal's eastern trade and the Mughal war fleets up to Guwahati, the gateway to Assam.

sea_head.evidence: Sonargaon was the capital and river port of eastern Bengal on the Meghna estuary system, reached by sea-going traders in the Sultanate period.

river_head.evidence: Mughal and Ahom fleets fought on the Brahmaputra at Guwahati in 1671, showing large-boat navigation up to this frontier trade town.

period_note: Before the 1780s shift the Brahmaputra flowed via Mymensingh to the Meghna near Sonargaon; Dhaka replaced Sonargaon after 1610. Dhubri, Goalpara and Hajo lie on the reach; Surma to Sylhet is a possible extra branch.

reason: Boat traffic was local and cut by rapids (Dummagudem barriers); its delta trade was coastal, so there is no substantial multi-place river cargo route in the period.

sea_head.evidence: Delta trade went through coastal ports such as Masulipatnam, not upriver.

period_note: Delta irrigation canals and steamer projects are 19th century.

reason: The Krishna is shallow and rocky with little historical boat cargo; trade used the coast and land routes.

sea_head.evidence: The delta port served sea trade only.

reason: Broach and Surat are estuary ports already coastal in game; upstream navigation was blocked by falls and shoals, so there is no multi-place river route.

sea_head.evidence: Surat on the lower Tapti was the chief Mughal sea port; Broach (broach) lies on the Narmada estuary.

reason: The Irrawaddy was Burma's main trade road, carrying rice, salt and goods from the delta past Prome, Pagan and Ava to Bhamo, the river terminus of the Yunnan caravan trade.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships called at Syriam and Dagon on the Yangon River, linked by delta creeks to the Irrawaddy; Syriam (thanlyin) has no river flag, so the nearest river location dagon is used.

river_head.evidence: Bhamo, historically Man Maw, is the highest regularly navigable point of the river and the transfer point for the China trade.

period_note: Ava (on the pinya/sagaing locations), Pagan, Prome (pyay), Myanaung and Hinthada lie on the reach. The narrow defiles above Mandalay are navigable and not treated as obstacles. Bassein (pathein) was a second delta sea port on the western distributary.

reason: Pegu itself is a coastal location in game (no river flag) and the Bago River is a short tidal creek, so it adds no multi-place route.

sea_head.evidence: Pegu was reached by sea ships via the Bago estuary in the 15th-16th centuries before silting.

reason: A dangerous tidal bore at the mouth and shoals limited it to local small-craft traffic.

sea_head.evidence: The Sittaung estuary is known for one of the world's strongest tidal bores.

period_note: Taungoo (taungoo) was reached overland or by small boats.

reason: The Chao Phraya carried Siam's foreign trade to Ayutthaya and the rice and forest-goods traffic from the northern towns down to the capital.

sea_head.evidence: Foreign sea-going ships sailed up the Chao Phraya to Ayutthaya, whose river channel the kings shortened with canals from 1538.

river_head.evidence: Nakhon Sawan sits where the Ping and Nan join to form the Chao Phraya and was the gateway of river traffic to the northern towns.

head.evidence: Phitsanulok on the Nan was Ayutthaya's northern royal seat and a river-boat town linked to the capital.

period_note: Bangkok/Thonburi (customs post) lies below Ayutthaya. The upper Ping to Chiang Mai had rapids and is left out.

reason: The lower Mekong carried Cambodia's trade: sea junks and European ships reached Phnom Penh/Lovek, and river craft went up to Kratie and Stung Treng below the Khone Falls.

sea_head.evidence: Chinese junks and Dutch and Portuguese ships came up the Mekong to the Phnom Penh-Lovek capital area in the 16th-17th centuries.

river_head.evidence: Boat traffic ran up to Stung Treng; the Khone Falls just above stopped through navigation, and goods for Laos were portaged around them.

branches.river: Tonle Sap (river and lake) to Angkor

head.evidence: Boats went from the Mekong at Phnom Penh up the Tonle Sap river and across the great lake to Angkor; Lovek (longvek) on the Tonle Sap river was the capital 1528-1594.

obstacles.name: Sambor/Preapatang rapids
obstacles.evidence: Rapids between Kratie and Stung Treng were passable at high water only; kracheh is the nearest tagged location.

obstacles.name: Khone Falls (upstream limit)
obstacles.evidence: The Khone Falls just above Stung Treng are the main reason the Mekong is not fully navigable; they bound the reach.

period_note: Van Wuysthoff (1641) went from Lovek to Vientiane by boat with portages, so Laos was reachable but not by through navigation; Laos Mekong reaches are left out. Prey Nokor/Saigon is on a separate river.

reason: The Red River linked Thang Long, the Dai Viet capital, with the sea and the delta; foreign merchants traded at Pho Hien and river craft carried their goods on to Ke Cho.

sea_head.evidence: Pho Hien was the river port where foreign ships stopped from the 16th century as the gateway to the capital's trade; khoai_chau is the tagged location at its coordinates.

river_head.evidence: Thang Long/Ke Cho, the capital and main market, was reached by river boats from Pho Hien; the VOC kept a factory there 1637-1700.

period_note: Traffic above Hanoi toward Yunnan grew mainly after 1600 and in the 19th century; left out.

reason: Hue only became the capital in the late 1600s-1802 and the river is short, so it adds no period cargo route; no Hue tag was found.

sea_head.evidence: No Hue location exists; dien_ban is the nearest coastal location, given only for completeness.

reason: The Musi carried Palembang's trade: sea-going ships reached the city and river craft brought pepper and forest produce down from the uplands.

sea_head.evidence: Palembang on the Musi, some distance inland, has been the river port of south Sumatra since Srivijaya and was reached by sea-going ships.

river_head.evidence: Pepper and forest goods came down the Musi from the uluan uplands to Palembang by boat; the upper-Musi location is a sensible terminus, not a single historic town.

period_note: Head is low confidence; the Ogan, Komering and Lematang tributaries also fed Palembang but are left out.

reason: Jambi's pepper port was reached by sea ships (Portuguese, English and Dutch factories), and the Batang Hari carried upland Minangkabau gold and pepper down past Muara Tebo.

sea_head.evidence: Jambi lies well inland on the Batang Hari and was the port for foreign pepper traders.

river_head.evidence: Dharmasraya on the upper Batang Hari was the Malayu capital in the 13th-14th centuries and the river link to the Minangkabau highlands.

period_note: Pepper traffic peaked in the 1600s; river head chosen at the upper-river political centre (batang_tebo is the intermediate stop).

reason: The Barito carried Banjar trade: Banjarmasin was a pepper port for foreign ships, and the earlier kingdom Negara Daha traded through its river port Muara Bahan.

sea_head.evidence: Banjarmasin, near the Barito mouth, was the port reached by sea-going pepper traders from the 16th century.

river_head.evidence: Negara Daha (14th-16th century) kept its trading port at Muara Bahan on the Barito.

head.evidence: The Negara Daha capital at Muhara Hulak, Negara, lay up the Negara tributary from Muara Bahan.

period_note: Low-medium confidence for the branch (in-game river level 2); upper Barito to Muara Teweh (teweh) was forest-produce traffic only.

reason: Before Pontianak (1771) the Kapuas carried only modest forest-produce and gold traffic between small river sultanates (Sanggau, Sintang); weakest case for a minimal set.

sea_head.evidence: Pontianak at the mouth was founded in 1771; the river is today the main waterway of West Kalimantan.

period_note: If a Borneo river is wanted later, Kapuas (sanggau, sintang) is a candidate for the 18th-19th century.

reason: Kutai's trade on the Mahakam was mostly small-craft forest produce; its centres Kutai Lama and later Tenggarong (1782) were modest ports.

sea_head.evidence: Kutai Lama at the delta was the Kutai Kartanegara seat before Tenggarong.

period_note: Optional addition: Kutai Lama -> Tenggarong -> Muara Kaman (muarakaman).

reason: The Pahang carried gold and tin by small boats to Pekan; volume and length of traffic were small.

sea_head.evidence: The Pahang sultanate's seat at Pekan is at the river mouth.

reason: Only about 25 km long between Manila Bay and Laguna de Bay, and Manila/Tondo have no river flag in game.

sea_head.evidence: Manila sits at the Pasig mouth on Manila Bay.
